summary: The note explores how Lunar New Year customs reflect folklore themes of unity and collective strength. It covers the legend of Nian, reunion dinner foods, the dragon dance, the Lantern Festival, modern adaptations like Chengdu's Moonlight Bazaar, and school lessons on folklore. It concludes that preserving these traditions offers lasting value in shared endeavor.
one_line: Lunar New Year customs, from the Nian legend to dragon dances and lanterns, embody folklore's lessons of unity and collective strength.
key_facts: Lunar New Year, or Spring Festival, begins on the first new moon between January 21 and February 20.
In 2024 the festivities commence on February 10, starting the year of the Dragon in the Chinese zodiac.
In folklore, Nian was a ferocious beast that devoured everything in its path once a year at the start of the New Year.
Villagers learned Nian feared loud noises, bright lights and the color red, which led to fireworks, red lanterns and red decorations.
The Lim family of Singapore gathered for a reunion dinner with fish for surplus and abundance, dumplings for wealth, and noodles for longevity.
Dr. June Tan, an archivist and cultural historian, said festive dishes are 'physical embodiments of the community's hopes and dreams.'
The dragon, a divine beast in Chinese mythology, represents power, strength and good luck.
The dragon dance troupe 'Eastern Serpents', led by choreographer Fei Long, performed in Beijing in February 2024.
Fei Long called the dragon dance 'a unifying force' that depends on each individual and the unity of the group.
The Lantern Festival (Yuan Xiao Jie) falls on the fifteenth day of the first lunar month, February 25 in 2024, marking the first full moon of the year.
In Pingxi, Taiwan, thousands of lanterns carrying wishes are released; a legend tells of a world saved from destruction by lantern light.
Liu Wei organized a night market at Chengdu's Moonlight Bazaar in 2024, where artisans and tech entrepreneurs displayed crafts and gadgets side by side.
Teacher Naomi Sato in Yokohama's Chinatown, Japan, uses Lunar New Year stories in her curriculum, and children re-enact battles against Nian.
